This drama, titled *The Little Clay Cart* (*Mṛcchakaṭika*), was composed by the illustrious Śūdraka. It is a work that delights the hearts of all people and is filled with various sentiments. It is a composition that brings joy to the ears of the learned and is worthy of being performed before an assembly of connoisseurs. Therefore, let us begin the performance. (He begins the prologue. Director: (To the actress) My dear, what is the name of this drama? Actress: Noble sir, it is called *The Little Clay Cart*. Director: (With wonder) Oh, how wonderful! What a magnificent title! For this drama is indeed like a little clay cart; it is small yet carries a great weight of meaning. Furthermore, it is as if it were made of clay, for it is fashioned from the very essence of the earth—the human heart. And just as a little cart can traverse many paths, so too does this drama lead the audience through a vast variety of emotions. Truly, it is a masterpiece. (He continues with the prologue. Director: (Addressing the actress) My dear, who is the hero of this play? Actress: Noble sir, he is Charudatta. Director: (With admiration) Ah, what a name! He is indeed a jewel among men. His virtues are as pure as crystal, his conduct is as firm as a mountain, and his compassion is as vast as the ocean. He is a man whose fame has spread throughout the world, a man who is the very embodiment of righteousness. Truly, he is the hero of this drama. (He continues with the prologue. Director: (Addressing the actress) My dear, who is the heroine of this play? Actress: Noble sir, she is Vasantasenā. Director: (With wonder) Oh, how wonderful! What a magnificent heroine! She is like a lotus born from the mud of the world, yet untouched by its impurities. She is like a moon rising from the darkness of night, illuminating the hearts of all. She is a woman whose beauty is peerless, whose grace is incomparable, and whose charm is beyond description. Truly, she is the heroine of this drama. (He continues with the prologue. Director: (Addressing the actress) My dear, what is the central theme of this play? Actress: Noble sir, it is the triumph of love over adversity. Director: (With delight) Ah, what a beautiful theme! It is a story of how true love, though tested by many trials, ultimately prevails. It is a tale of how two souls, separated by fate, find their way back to one another through the power of destiny. Truly, it is a drama that teaches the value of love and the endurance of the human spirit. (He concludes the prologue. Director: (Turning to the audience) O worthy ones, please grant me your attention. This drama, *The Little Clay Cart*, is now ready to be performed. May it bring you joy and wisdom. (He bows. Bharata— what do the physicians say of him?

"What food does he eat, and what is his bed? Sūta replied: "He eats nothing, sleeping upon the ground."

My heart throbs; drive the chariot! || 1 ||

(Restraining the speed of the chariot) Oh, how great indeed is the speed of the chariot!—
these trees seem to run, as the range of vision is diminished by the rapid motion of the vehicle.
The river-like water of the chariot wheels falls upon the rim of the earth's circumference;
the spokes are no longer visible as they are lost in the speed, and the circle of the chariot seems to stand still.

Long-lived one! Because of the moisture [from the trees], Ayodhyā must surely be surrounded by trees.

Oh, how indeed my mind hastens, longing to see my own kin! For now, as it were, my head has fallen at my father's feet; I am filled with affection, as if raised up by the King himself.
As if my brothers had arrived in haste, and as if my mothers were drenching me with tears, [he thought]:
"He is like [me]," "He is great," and "He is tall."
I was praised by him with service as if by servants; there, I observed both the dress and the speech of the son of Sumitrā as if they were a mockery of myself. || 3 ||

Of these images, which have been fashioned by divine seers and yet possess the trust of men—what indeed is this hymn of four deities? Or rather, let them be whatever they may be;
for there is a great joy in my heart.
Granted, it would be better to simply bow one's head, saying "It is a deity."
But the *vārṣala* salutation is that in which the deity is worshipped without mantras. || 5 ||

"I shall know" (entering).
Bharata:—
Homage!
The temple attendant:
Indeed, indeed, no salutation should be performed.

By what is this prohibition established? It is by the power of a restrictive rule (niyama).

Thus, sirs, you are Kṣatriyas. Now, what is the name of your lineage?

Bharata:—(With joy) "The Ikṣvākus! These are those lords of Ayodhyā;

these are they who go forth as reinforcements for the gods in the destruction of the city of the Asuras; these are they who, together with their cities and provinces, proceed to the world of Śakra by virtue of their own meritorious deeds.
These are they who have attained the entire earth conquered by the strength of their own arms; these are they who, for a long time, were not overtaken by Death as it sought its prey.
"O sir! By chance, indeed, I have obtained a great fruit. Pray, tell me, who is this honorable gentleman?
The temple-priest:
"This is indeed King Dilīpa, the performer of the Viśvajit sacrifice in which all his wealth was bestowed as a gift, and the blazing lamp of Dharma."
Bharata:
Homage to you, who are devoted to dharma! Pray, tell me, who is this honorable person?
Temple-keeper: [He speaks.]
This is indeed Raghu, whose voice of "auspicious day" (*puṇyāha*) was raised by many thousands of Brahmins during his lying down and rising.
Bharata:

Oh, how powerful is Death! He has transgressed even this protection. Homage to the one for whom the fruit of sovereignty was announced by the people of the Brahmin caste! Let it be told: who is this honorable person?

The Temple Guardian: This, indeed, is Aja, who has cast off the burden of kingship out of despondency at being separated from his beloved; he is one whose passion is stilled by constant ritual ablutions after sacrifices.
Bharata: [Listens.]

"Homage be to this praiseworthy remorse! (Looking at the image of Daśaratha and becoming distressed: "O! With a mind distracted by great respect, I clearly did not perceive [who this was]. Let it be told: who, pray, is this venerable one?
Temple-keeper:—
This is Dilīpa.
Bharata—[he is] the grandfather of the Great King. What then? What then?
The temple-keeper:
His Highness Raghu.
Bharata: [Listens.]
The grandfather of the great king. And then?
The temple-attendant:
His Majesty Aja.
Bharata: "The father of my father. Devakulika: "What? What?"
"This is Dilīpa, this is Raghu, this is Aja;

The temple-keeper:

The temple-keeper: Stay!

Alas, father! (Faints and falls; then regaining consciousness: O heart, have your desire fulfilled! Listen to that death of my father about which you feared, and meanwhile, summon your fortitude.

"Noble sir!

Bharata:
Indeed, indeed! I am Bharata, the son of Daśaratha, not of Kaikeyī. Temple-keeper:
[He understands.]

Bharata: ...
"How? How? Has even the Noble One gone to the forest? (He falls into a double swoon. Temple-attendant: "Prince! Take heart, take heart!"
Bharata:—
(Recovering his composure) Ayodhyā has become a wilderness, abandoned by both my father and my brother.
Afflicted by thirst, I run after you like one pursuing a river whose waters have dried up.

"Noble sir! Hearing this in detail produces steadfastness in me; therefore, let it all be told without omission. The temple-keeper replied: "Listen, for when His Majesty King Daśaratha was being consecrated, His Majesty Rāma’s mother reportedly said this to you:"
Bharata: Stop!
Remembering that fault regarding the bride-price, it was said by me, "Let my son be king."
"O son! Take heart through that fortitude and go to the forest"—thus was even the noble one addressed.
Seeing him with his bark garment bound on, having met such an untimely death, the king has indeed departed; alas, the ministers are now casting reproaches upon me, as if they were my equals. 11.
(Offstage) Move aside, noble sirs! Move aside! (Move aside, noble sirs; move aside!
The temple-keeper:
(Looking) Ah!
The queens have indeed arrived at the very moment their son has fallen into a swoon;
for the touch of a mother's hand is like a handful of water to one who is without water.
(Then enter the queens and Sumantra.

This way, ladies, this way.
This is the palace of that king in effigy; it is our lofty abode, the like of which is rare even among palaces.

(Entering and looking around) Ladies! Indeed, indeed, you must not enter!

(Recovering slightly) Noble sir!

And now, what is the condition of my mothers?
The Queens:— Child! This is our condition. (They remove their veils. (Child! This is our condition.

"O ladies! Let your longing be restrained.

Prince, what else? I am Sumantra, being pursued by the faults of long life.
Mocked by my ingratitude,
for when that king has perished, I live as the charioteer of an empty chariot. (15)

"Certainly; this is the noble lady Kausalyā, the mother of the venerable Rāma.

"Mother! I, who have committed no offense, offer my salutations."

(To himself: I feel as if I have been insulted by him. (Aloud: I am favored by this. And then? And then? Sumantra: This is the noble lady Sumitrā, the mother of the honorable Lakṣmaṇa.

Mother, I have been deceived by Lakṣmaṇa; I offer my salutations.

"My child! May you be a partaker of glory!

Bharata: [He faints.]
(Rising up in anger: Ah, you wicked woman!
Standing between my mother and my maternal grandmother, you do not shine;
you are like a tiny stream forced between the Ganges and the Yamunā.
Kaikeyī:
My child! What have I done?
Bharata: — [continues]

"What have you done? you ask. Indeed, by you, we have been joined with infamy; the noble king with a tattered garment; the entire city of Ayodhyā with a death in the home and incessant wailing; Lakṣmaṇa with the wild beasts;
our mothers with grief for their beloved sons; and our own selves with the exhaustion of the journey for our daughters-in-law and with harsh words of reproach—alas! 17.
Kausalyā:
My son! Why do you not salute your mother, standing as you are in the midst of all formal etiquette?
Bharata: [He remains silent.]
"Mother! "O Mother! You alone are my mother! O Mother! I salute you! Kausalyā:
"No, no! This is your mother. (No, this is your mother.)
Bharata:
It was so in the past, but not now. Let your ladyship observe:
having abandoned affection, [those whose] faults have been transferred through their conduct—
Sons who were previously not sons are now made such; I shall establish a new law in the world: a mother who obstructs her husband is no longer a mother.
Kaikeyī:
My son! It was spoken by me thus while protecting the word of truth of the Great King.
Bharata: ...
"What? What?
Kaikeyī: "Let my son become king. (Let my son become king.)
Bharata: Now, who is this noble one of yours?
My father’s son by a non-primary wife is not being consecrated in due order.
If they were not beloved brothers, it would not be pleasing to the subjects. || 19 ||
Kaikeyī:
My son! Surely she, who is greedy for the bride-price, must be questioned.
Bharata: [Listens.]
"Deprived of the glory of his kingdom by bark garments, he was ordered by you to dwell in the forest on foot with his wife; this very thing was cited as an example regarding the toll. (20)
Kaikeyī: My child!
I shall inform you of the place and the time.
Bharata: — [listens]
If you have greed for infamy, what is the point of praising us?
And what of your thirst for the fruit of kingship—would the lord of men not grant it? Or is this title "the King’s Mother" the one you desire?
Speak, lady! Is it true that the noble one is not your son?
A grievous deed has been done by you;
desiring the kingdom, you did not spare the king his life, and you sent your eldest son away to the forest.
Alas, having seen that the daughter of Janaka is as fragile as a lute-string, the Creator must have fashioned this heart of yours to be as hard as adamant.
Sumantra:
Prince! These two, Vasiṣṭha and Vāmadeva, together with the ministers, having placed the consecration before them, have come out to meet you and announce:
"Just as cattle, when deprived of their cowherd and left unprotected, go to ruin," [so it would be for us without you].
In this way, indeed, subjects deprived of a king go to ruin. || 23 ||
Bharata: Let the subjects follow me. Sumantra: [As directed.]
"Where will you go after relinquishing the consecration?
Bharata:
"As for the consecration—let it be bestowed here upon her honor."

Where will you go, sir? Bharata:
I shall go there where he who is dear to Lakṣmaṇa resides; without him, Ayodhyā is not Ayodhyā—only that place where Rāghava is truly Ayodhyā.

"Friend! Out of curiosity, we have seen the noble son Bharata.

Listen! Having dismissed the consecration brought by the subjects, the prince has gone to Rāma’s penance grove.

the son of the king who crushed the pride of the lord of the Daityas.

Bharata: And has the venerable father gone to the forest together with the venerable mother? Sumantra:
Ah! This is the lady, the daughter of King Janaka.
This is that female energy born from the depths of the sacrificial ground, a manifest proof of the ascetic power of King Janaka, the lord of men. (14)
"Noble lady! I, Bharata, salute you.
Rāma—(with joy): "Come, come, O prince of the Ikṣvākus! Hail! May you be long-lived!"
Spread out your chest, as wide as the panels of a door, and embrace me with your two very broad arms;
lift up this face, which is like a digit of the autumn moon, and gladden this body consumed by its own affliction. 15.
Bharata:
I am favored. Sumantra:—
(Approaching: Victory to the long-lived one!
Rāma:—Alas, father!

Having previously gone forth with his own armies at the time of the assault, he who was renowned among the gods and the asuras alike for his prowess in battle—that glorious Indra, now dwelling in heaven after casting off his body, does he delight in the company of his own ancestors, the lords of men, while you, his beloved, remain here full of affection? (17)
Sumantra — (with sorrow):
The death of the lord of men and your own exile...
Having experienced Bharata’s despondency and the helplessness of my lineage, as well as various other unbearable hardships, my life has committed many offenses against my virtues.
Sītā:
While my noble husband is already weeping, my father makes him weep even more.
Rāma: [Listens.]
O Maithilī! Here, I shall compose myself. Child Lakṣmaṇa! Fetch some water, then.
Lakṣmaṇa: As my noble brother commands.
Bharata:
Noble brother! This is truly not right. I shall attend upon you in due order; I myself will go. (Taking the water-pot, he exits and re-enters. Here is the water.
Rāma: ...
(Having sipped water) Maithilī! Lakṣmaṇa’s service is indeed being neglected.
Sītā:
Noble Lord! Surely he too must be attended to.
Rāma:
Indeed, let Lakṣmaṇa serve me here; let Bharata serve me while staying there.
Bharata: [Silence].
May the Noble One be gracious.
I shall remain here with my body, but I shall remain there through my actions; thus, your kingdom will have its protection secured by my name alone. (19)
Rāma:
Child, son of Kaikeyī! Do not speak thus.
I have come to the forest by my father’s command.
"Not out of pride, nor out of fear, nor out of delusion, my child;
yet I tell you, our lineage possesses true wealth—how is it that you proceed upon a base path? (20)
Sumantra:
Now then, where shall the consecration water be kept? Rāma: [He remains silent.]
Let it rest right there where my mother spoke it.
Bharata:
May the noble one be gracious! Noble brother, enough now of striking at a wound.
O virtuous one! Your birth is indeed my own birth; for he, your father, was truly a man of profound intellect, and he was my father as well.
O noble man! Among men, the fault of the mother is no fault at all.
O Giver of Boons! Behold now the distressed Bharata exactly as he is.
Sītā:
Noble Lord! Bharata is deliberating most piteously. What is it that the Noble Lord is contemplating now?
Rāma: O Maithilī,
I think of that king who has departed to the world of the gods.
Alas! Woe to the power of Fate regarding these supreme men, since this treasury of virtues, possessing such distinguished qualities, has not been seen by him! (22)
Child, son of Kaikeyī!
Truly, I am gratified by you; you are pure of soul, and I am subject to the power of your words, for I have been conquered by your renowned virtues.
However, it is not fitting for you to make that word of the king false; rather, having produced someone like yourself, let your father be the one who speaks falsely.
Bharata:
O King! May I remain here at the soles of your feet until the conclusion of your holy observance.
Rāma: Not so! Let the king attain success through his own meritorious deeds;
I adjure you by my own self if you do not protect your own kingdom. 24.
Bharata:
An unsurpassed answer has been spoken. Very well; on this condition, I shall protect the kingdom for you.
Rāma: [Silence]
"My child! What is the agreement? Bharata replied: "I wish to receive back your kingdom, which has been entrusted to my hands, at the end of fourteen years."
Rāma: So be it.
Bharata:—
Noble sir! I have heard! Noble lady, I have heard! Father! I have heard!
We all—indeed, we too—are listeners.
Bharata:
Noble brother! I wish to ask for another favor as well.
Rāma: [Listens.]
"My child! What do you desire? What shall I give? What shall I perform?
Bharata replied:
"The two sandals worn upon your feet, [grant them] to me."
"Grant these to him who bows with his head lowered;
until you have achieved your purpose, I shall remain subservient to these two. (25)
Rāma:
— (Welcoming him) Ah, indeed! Even after a very long time, some measure of fame has been acquired by me.
In a very short time, it has been gathered today by Bharata.
Sītā:
Noble Lord! Surely the first request must be granted to Bharata.
Rāma: [Listens.]
"So be it; let them be accepted. (He offers the sandals.
Bharata:
"I am favored. (Taking them) "Noble brother! I wish to pour the consecration water upon these here."
Rāma:
Father! Let everything that Bharata desires be done.
Sumantra:—
"As the venerable Bharata commands!
(To himself) Alas! Oh!
I am a son worthy of the trust of my kinsmen, beloved by the citizens and the people, capable of withstanding public scrutiny, dear to the king who dwells in heaven,
endowed with virtuous conduct, highly esteemed by my brothers who are rich in merit, and a great vessel of fame.
In conversations, he is the beloved topic for those who possess virtue and have won the affection [of others]. (27)
Rāma:
Dear son, son of Kaikeyī! That which is called a kingdom must not be neglected even for a moment. Therefore, let the prince return this very day for the sake of victory.
Sītā: [Silence]
"Indeed, Prince Bharata will depart this very day.
Rāma:
Enough of this excessive affection! Let the prince return this very day for victory.
Bharata:
Noble brother, I shall depart this very day.
The citizens in the city will remain full of hope, longing for the sight of you.
I shall bring them joy by beholding your favor.
Sumantra:— Long-lived one! What must I do now?
Rāma:—
"Father! Let the prince be protected like a great king.
Sumantra: "If I live, I shall strive to do so."
Rāma:
Child, son of Kaikeyī, please mount the chariot ahead of me.
Bharata: [Mounts.]
"As the Noble One commands. (They mount the chariot.
Rāma:
Maithilī! This way, please. Dear Lakṣmaṇa! This way, please. We shall accompany Bharata even as far as the gateway of the hermitage.
(Thus they all exit.
The Fourth Act. (Then enter Sītā and an ascetic woman.)
Sītā:

Noble lady, the hermitage has been strewn with offerings and flowers and swept clean; the ritual for the gods has been performed according to the resources of this hermitage. Therefore, until my noble husband returns, I shall honor these young trees by providing them with water.
"Therefore, until my noble husband returns, I shall tend to these young trees with the gift of water.
Ascetic:
May he meet with no obstacles. (May there be no hindrance for him.)
Rāma:—
(With sorrow) Having abandoned that lovely city of Ayodhyā, which was bereft of both my preceptor and myself, he has come into my presence, having even undertaken my entire consecration.
Furthermore, Bharata, a treasury of virtues, was sent back to that very place for the sake of protection; alas! The king alone bears this exceedingly great burden. || 1 ||
(Reflecting) This is indeed so. Now, for the sake of dispelling such grief, I shall go to see Maithilī, who is like a wife to this household of circumstances. Where, then, has Vaidehī gone?

(Walking about and looking) Ah! These recently watered bases of trees indicate that Maithilī has not gone far. For instance, the water whirls around the trees, forming eddies and remaining covered with foam.
These birds, though fallen into thirst, do not drink the turbid water;
the frogs leap onto dry land; the insects in the water-filled hole [seek] the opening; and the trees, once encircled by new boughs, now show at their roots the mark of the water's depletion.
(Looking) Ah, here is Vaidehī! Oh, how painful!
That hand of hers which would grow weary even while holding a mirror does not feel any exhaustion as she carries this water-jar.
Alas! The forest, which is naturally tender for women, makes it as hard as a whetstone when combined with the creepers.
(Approaching) Maithilī! Is your asceticism prospering?
Sītā:
Oh, it is my noble husband! Victory to my noble husband!
Rāma:
Maithilī! If there is no obstacle to your dharma, please be seated.
Sītā: —
"As my noble lord commands. (She sits down.
Rāma: Maithilī! I see you as if you were seeking a reply. What is this?
Sītā:
What is this change in the complexion of my noble husband’s face, which seems as if his heart were empty with grief?
Rāma: [He speaks.]
O Maithilī, your anxiety is indeed justified!
While my body is already pierced by the shafts of Death, the wound in my heart remains just as it was;
the blows from the arrows of grief, bearing manifold fruits, fall again and again upon that very same spot. (4)
Sītā:
What kind of distress, pray, does my noble husband feel?
Rāma: —

"Tomorrow is the annual *śrāddha* ceremony for our revered father. According to the specific ritual injunctions, the ancestors desire the performance of the *nivapana* rite. Therefore, I am reflecting on how I shall accomplish this. Or rather—let them go by whatever means they please;
for they themselves know my condition."
Nevertheless, I desire to perform worship for my father as well as for Rāma in a manner that is befitting.
Rāma: O Maithilī!
Having seen these fruits, arranged by our own hands upon the darbha grass...
And when reminded of his forest exile, my father wept even there.
(Then enters Rāvaṇa in the guise of a wandering mendicant.
Rāvaṇa: Ho there! This is I!
Having assumed this form, which is both determinate and indeterminate in nature, and having deceived Rāghava— who harbors enmity toward me like a butcher toward a donkey—
I shall depart like a stream of sacrificial oblation deprived of its voice and its path.
Desiring to abduct that daughter of King Janaka, I am departing.
(Walking about and looking ahead) This is the entrance to Rāma’s hermitage. (As I descend...
(He descends. While I too shall perform the rites of hospitality for a guest—I am a guest—who is there, sir?
Rāma—
(Having heard this: Welcome to the guest!
Rāvaṇa:
Well said; indeed, your form has been correctly identified by your voice.
Rāma—(Looking) Ah, the Blessed One! Blessed One, I salute you.
Rāvaṇa—
Hail!
Rāma:
Venerable sir, please be seated on this seat.
Rāvaṇa:—(To himself) How is it that I feel as if I have been commanded by him? (Aloud) Certainly. (He sits down.
Rāma:—
Maithilī! Bring water for the Blessed One.
Sītā: As the noble son commands. (Exit and re-enter. Here is the water. (As the noble son commands. Here is the water.)
Rāma:
Serve the venerable one with devotion.
Sītā: [Does so.]
"As my noble lord commands.
Rāvaṇa:—
(Becoming agitated by the manifestation of the magic power) Very well, very well.
For she alone among women on earth is an Arundhatī,
by whom you, her husband, are spoken of with honor by all women.
Rāma:
In that case, bring it; I myself shall attend to it.
Rāvaṇa: [Silence.]
Ah! I do not avoid the shadow, nor do I bypass the body [of my guest]. Indeed, compliance with one’s words is the very essence of honoring a guest. I have been honored. Pray, be seated.
Rāma:— Very well. (He sits down.)

Rāvaṇa:—(To himself) I too shall now perform the customary conduct of a Brāhmaṇa. (Aloud) O sir! I am of the Kāśyapa lineage; I have studied the Vedas with their limbs and sub-limbs, as well as the Dharmaśāstra of Manu, the Yogaśāstra of Maheśvara, the Arthaśāstra of Bṛhaspati, the Nyāyaśāstra of Medhātithi, and the Śrāddhakalpa of Pracetas.
Rāma:
What? How so? "The ritual for the ancestral offerings (śrāddha-kalpa)"? Rāvaṇa:—
"Having transcended all the Vedas, a longing for the *Śrāddhakalpa* has been shown. What is this?
Rāma:
"O Blessed One! Since the state of having a father has been lost, this is now the traditional scripture (*āgama*)."
Rāvaṇa:
Enough of avoiding the matter; may you ask. Rāma: [asks].
"Bhagavān! At the time of the ritual of scattering the offerings, with what do I satisfy the ancestors?
Rāvaṇa replied: "The entire śrāddha offering, when given with faith."
Rāma: Holy sir! It has been abandoned out of disrespect. I ask for a specific reason. Rāvaṇa:—

Listen: among grasses, *darbha*; among herbs, sesame; among vegetables, peas; among fish, the large *śaphara*; among birds, the *vārdhrāṇasa*; among animals, the cow or the rhinoceros—these are prescribed for human beings. Rāma: * *Darbha* is a type of sacred grass used in ritual ceremonies. * *Tila* refers to sesame seeds. * *Kalāya* denotes a kind of pea or lentil. * *Mahāśaphara* is a large species of fish. * *Vārdhrāṇasa* is a specific type of bird (often identified as a kind of crane). * *Gauḥ* means a cow. * *Khaṅga* refers to a rhinoceros. Rāma: [continues]...
"O Blessed One! By the word 'or' (vā), it is understood that there is something else as well.
Rāvaṇa: "There is that which is to be accomplished through supernatural power (prabhāva)."
Rāma:
Holy sir! This indeed is my resolve:
if this will accomplish both [ends], then let there be the presence of both.
Either the bow [rests] upon asceticism when it is weary, or asceticism [rests] upon the bow when it is weary.
Rāvaṇa:
They exist; they dwell upon the Himavat. Rāma: [They do.]
"From there? From there?
Rāvaṇa said:

"On the seventh peak of the Himavat, there are deer named Kāñcanapārśvas; they drink the waters of the Gaṅgā as it falls upon the head of Sthāṇu who stands before their eyes, their backs are dark like lapis lazuli, and they possess a speed equal to the wind."

By those [offerings], the great sages such as the Vaikhānasas, Vālakhilyas, and Naimiśīyas—who cause the ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) to flourish through the perishing of [oblations] that appear as soon as they are thought of—the ancestors, when gratified, obtain the fruit of sons; indeed, casting off old age, they go to the sky, shining brightly.
They attain residence in celestial chariots equal to the gods, and they are not forcibly dragged away by transitory sense-objects.
Rāma: Maithilī!
Take leave of the fawns and the trees that have become like your own children.
The Vindhya forest shall be your friends and the beloved creepers;
I shall dwell among them in the groves of the Himalayan mountains,
which are colored as if by forests of glowing medicinal herbs.
Sītā:
As my noble husband commands.
Rāvaṇa:—
O son of Kausalyā! Enough of this excessive longing; they are not visible to mortal men.
Rāma:
Venerable sir, do they dwell in the Himavat?
Rāvaṇa:
Indeed so. Rāma:—
Therefore, let your honor behold this:
either the Himalayas will show those golden deer to me,
or, pierced by the force of my arrow, it shall become like Krauñca.
Rāvaṇa:
(With a greeting) Ah, how truly unbearable is his arrogance!
Rāma:—
(Looking toward the quarters. Ah! It appears like a flash of lightning. Rāvaṇa:
(Aloud) O son of Kausalyā, while you remain right here, Himavat pays you honor. Here is Kāñcanapārśva.
Rāma:
This is an increase in fortune for the Blessed One.
Sītā:—
By good fortune, my noble lord prospers!
Rāma: No, no.
"These are my father's good fortunes that he has come here of his own accord; for he truly deserves honor. O Maithilī, speak thus to Lakṣmaṇa. (13)
Sītā:
Noble Lord! Has it not been commanded that Saumitri should go out to meet the family preceptor upon his return from the pilgrimage?
Rāma:
In that case, I myself shall go.
Sītā:—
"Noble Lord! What shall I do? Rāma:
"Serve the Blessed One."
Sītā:
As my noble husband commands.
(Rāma exits.)
Rāvaṇa:
Ah! Here comes Rāghava, taking up his bow. Now, disregarding the worship [offered to him], Rāghava sees a deer running and strings his bow.
Oh, what strength! Oh, what heroism! Oh, what courage! Oh, what speed!
By the few syllables "Rā-ma," this entire world is pervaded in its proper place.

This is the deer; having leaped over the range of my arrow with a single bound, it has entered the dense forest. Sītā—(To herself: Since I am separated from my noble husband, fear arises within me here.
Rāvaṇa:— (To himself) ... [is] carried away by illusion.
Sītā:
Until I enter the leaf-hut. (She attempts to go. (As she enters the leaf-hut.
Rāvaṇa:—
(Assuming his own form: Sītā! Stay, stay!
Sītā—(With fear: Ah, who is this now?
Rāvaṇa: Do you not know?
By him, in battle, the gods along with the hosts of Dānavas, headed by Śakra, were always conquered.
Having seen the disfigurement of Śūrpaṇakhā and heard that her two brothers have been slain,
I, Rāvaṇa— out of pride, having enticed with deceptions the evil-minded Rāma who possesses immeasurable strength, and being intent on abducting you, O large-eyed one— have arrived here. (16)
Sītā:
Ah, he is named Rāvaṇa! (She sets out. (Ah, he is named Rāvaṇa!
Rāvaṇa:—
"Āḥ! Having come within the range of Rāvaṇa's sight, where will you go?
Sītā:
"Noble Lord! Save me, save me! Saumitri! Save me, save me!"
"Save me!
Rāvaṇa:
Sītā, listen to my prowess!
Śakra was broken, the Lord of Wealth trembled, Soma was dragged away, and the Son of the Sun was crushed;
fie upon this heaven inhabited by terrified gods!
Blessed is the land where Sītā dwells.
Sītā:
Noble Lord! Save me, save me! Saumitri! Save me, save me!
Rāvaṇa:

Seek refuge with Rāma, or with Lakṣmaṇa, or even with King Daśaratha who dwells in heaven. What could possibly come of words addressed to those who rely on base men? Young deer do not dare to attack a tiger.
Sītā:
Noble Lord! Save me, save me! Saumitri! Save me, protect me!
Rāvaṇa:
"Why do you lament thus, O large-eyed one, considering me as your noble son?
This man of mine is endowed with vast power to fight."
Even with his host of fathers-in-law, Rāma is indeed powerless. || 19 ||
Sītā—
(With anger) You are cursed!
Rāvaṇa—
Hahaha! Oh, the splendor of this woman’s devotion to her husband!
For I, who leaped up with such speed, was not burned by the rays of the sun;
yet I have been burned by her with these measured syllables: "You are cursed! (20)
Sītā:
Noble Lord! Save me, save me!
Rāvaṇa:—
(Taking Sītā by the hand: O you ascetics dwelling in Janasthāna! Listen, listen, all of you!
This Ten-necked one is departing, having seized Sītā by force. If Rāma were devoted to the duty of a warrior (*kṣatradharma*), he would display his prowess.
Sītā:
Noble Lord! Save me, save me!
Rāvaṇa:—
(Walking about and looking around: Ah! Here comes Jaṭāyu, his fierce beak agitating the forest thickets as he is tossed by the wind from his own wings. Ah! Stay right there now!
With your body drenched in blood dripping from the wounds of your wings, severed by the weapons drawn by my arms, I shall lead you to the abode of Yama.
(They both exit.
The Fifth Act. (Then enter two aged ascetics.)
Both:—
May you protect us, may you protect us, sirs!
First:—
For here is the lord of the night-stalkers, who moves about at midnight, possessing the luster of a garland of blue lotuses and a smile with fangs as brilliant as white lotus stalks.
Like a doe, Sītā is being led away after having been humiliated. || 1 ||
The second [actor]:
This is indeed the noble Vaidehī,
appearing like a female serpent struggling.
Like a flowering creeper being shaken,
she is being forcibly led away from the penance grove by the wicked Ten-faced one, as if she were spiritual perfection itself being carried off.
Both:—
May you protect us, may you protect us, sirs!
First:—

(Looking upward) Ah! As soon as these words were spoken, Jaṭāyu, having summoned Rāvaṇa with the cry, "While I am standing here, where will you go to discharge your debt to Daśaratha?", has flown up into the sky.
Second Actor—There is Rāvaṇa, returning with his eyes rolling in rage.
First—
This is Rāvaṇa. Second—
This is Jaṭāyu. Both— Ah, this battle has commenced in the sky!
The first said: "Kāśyapa! Kāśyapa! Behold the power of the Lord of Carnivores!
Having surpassed the range of his own vigor with his two wings, he arrays himself for combat."
With his two snouts, he violently rubs and circles the sharp, immovable [surface];
with his claws, which are like sharp, painful thorns, he tears at the formidable interior of the chest,
just as a jagged rock is split from a mountain by the points of a thunderbolt.
Second:
Alas! Enraged, Rāvaṇa has struck the Lord of the Flesh-eaters with his sword in the region of his right shoulder.
Both: [Alas!]
Alas! His Honor Jaṭāyu has fallen here—our first [companion]!
Oh, what misery! This indeed is His Honor Jaṭāyu.
Having exerted the utmost effort commensurate with his own prowess,
and disregarding the enemy like a toy peacock,
he brushed aside the blazing splendor of the Lord of Night-stalkers.
He lay prostrate like a forest tree broken by the lord of serpents. || 4 ||
Both:—
Let this be our own [private] matter.
First:—
Kāśyapa! Come; we shall report this news to the venerable Rāghava.
Second:
Very well. This is the first course of action.
(They both exit.
Interlude. (Then the chamberlain enters.)
Chamberlain: Ho there! Who keeps the golden arched gateway unoccupied? (He enters.)
Pratihārī:
Noble sir! I am Vijayā. What should be done?
Kāñcukīya: [Listens.]
Vijayā! Let it be announced, let it be announced to Prince Bharata:
"His Majesty has indeed returned from Janasthāna, having set out there for the purpose of seeing Rāma. Portress: [Does so.]
"Noble sir! Has my father Sumantra returned having accomplished his purpose?
Chamberlain:
"Madam, I do not know."
"Upon seeing Sumantra arrive with his face parched by the fire of grief residing in his heart, my mind has now become deeply agitated. (5)
Pratihārī:
Noble sir! Having heard this, my heart is as if agitated. Kāñcukīya: [Listens.]
"Madam! Why do you stand there now? Let it be reported at once. Portress:
"Noble sir! I shall report this. (She exits. (Noble sir! I shall report this.)

Chamberlain: (Looking) Ah! Here comes His Highness Prince Bharata, his curiosity aroused by the arrival of Sumantra; he approaches this way, clad in garments of bark and rags, with his head adorned by a mass of matted hair.
He is this one:
He whose multitude of excellent virtues is renowned, who is the season for his adversaries, the ornament of the solar dynasty, and equal to the Lord of the Gods;
who stands ready to protect the entire earth by the power of his command, the illustrious one whose vehicle is like a noble, young elephant.
(Then enter Bharata and the female door-keeper.
Bharata:
Vijayā! Thus has the venerable Sumantra arrived.
Having previously gone to see the noble one while I was distressed by his gaze, and having returned after receiving his grace and his word,
why has the venerable Sumantra come here?
Rāma, who delights the eyes, intellect, and minds of all living beings.
Chamberlain: (Approaching) Victory to the Prince!
Bharata:—
"Now, in which place is the honorable Sumantra? The Chamberlain: "He is at the golden arched gateway."
Bharata:
In that case, let him be ushered in at once. Chamberlain: [Does so.]
"As the Prince commands. (Exit.
(Then enter Sumantra and the female door-keeper.
Sumantra:—
(With sorrow) Alas, what misery! Oh, what misery!
The death of the king has been experienced by me; the calamity that befell the king’s son was witnessed by me alone.
I have heard here of that destruction of Maithilī; it is as if my long life has committed many offenses against its own virtue.
Pratihārī:
(Pointing toward Sumantra) Come, come, noble sir! There is the master. Approach, noble sir. (Having approached: "Come, come, noble sir! Here is the master. Please approach, noble sir. Sumantra:—
(Approaching) Victory to the Prince!
Bharata:

Father! Have you seen him who has manifested paternal affection before the world? Have you seen the conduct of Arundhatī split in two? Have you seen that forest-dwelling with his brothers, which was undertaken without any selfish motive?
(Sumanta stands reflecting. Door-keeper:
The prince is indeed inquiring after the noble sir.
Sumantra:
My lady! Why me?
Bharata:—
(To himself) This is indeed a very great exertion; my heart has failed me from the heat. (Aloud) Has the venerable Sumantra returned from his journey?
Sumantra: Prince! At your command, I set out for Janasthāna to see Rāma; how could I have turned back midway?
Bharata:
Why indeed do they not show themselves, whether out of anger or out of shame? Sumantra: [He speaks.]
"O Prince! Whence could there be anger in those who are disciplined, or shame in those whose minds are composed?
